title: Bring the research station back online
description: A storm has silenced the research station. Restore its systems by investigating charge flow, energy and circuit faults.
audience: Learners approaching A-level physics, with optional GCSE bridges; curious adult explorers welcome
level: Introduction bridging GCSE to A-level DC circuits

skills.title: Explain closed-path charge flow and distinguish current from charge
skills.criterion: Correct mechanism prediction and applicable numeric/design task with correct units; at least two fresh independent opportunities, not completion count

skills.title: Interpret potential difference as energy transferred per unit charge
skills.criterion: Fresh independently marked energy-per-charge calculation and a causal distinction from current in a new circuit; at least two opportunities, not completion count

skills.title: Predict how ideal resistance changes current
skills.criterion: Use I = V/R with correct units on a fresh configuration and state the fixed-voltage condition; at least two independent opportunities

skills.title: Explain and predict current and potential difference in series and parallel paths
skills.criterion: Independently predict fresh branch and loop readings with correct units, and justify current and energy conservation in an unfamiliar arrangement; at least two fresh opportunities

nodes.title: Wake the beacon
nodes.prompt: The beacon is dark. Two links were opened during the storm. Make a complete conducting path to bring it online. Try either link first.
hints: Trace from one supply terminal, through the heater, and back to the other terminal.
A break anywhere in this single path stops the steady current. Find every break.
nodes.workedExample: Close both links. With the path complete, the 6 V supply drives 1 A through the 6 ohm heater. Reopening either link stops it; the heater has not used up charge.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

nodes.title: What if the return link opens?
nodes.prompt: The beacon is running. Predict the steady current near the supply after only the return link opens. Then test your idea.

options.text: It keeps flowing near the supply, but not after the gap.
options.feedback: Steady charge cannot keep piling up at the gap. A break interrupts the entire single path.

options.text: It falls because the heater consumes the charge.
options.feedback: The heater transfers energy from moving charge. Charge is conserved; the missing conducting path causes the stop.

options.text: It falls to zero throughout the path.
options.feedback: Yes. A return-side break interrupts the same complete path as a supply-side break.

hints: Follow the entire path, including the return side.
nodes.workedExample: In a single loop, removing a connection on either side of the load stops the steady current everywhere.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

nodes.title: Test the return-side fault
nodes.prompt: Open the return link and watch the meter. You can also compare opening the supply link, or restore the beacon again before leaving. The goal is a stopped current.
hints: Try the return link. Compare the source current with the reading across the heater.
nodes.workedExample: Open the return link. Current becomes 0 A, heater power 0 W. With just one break the source voltage appears across that break.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

nodes.title: A new instrument, a new fault
nodes.prompt: A separate thermometer has one conducting loop: supply → resistor → return. Its current was 0.4 A. A wire breaks after the resistor. What is the new steady current before the resistor?

options.feedback: A single break is not a half-resistance adjustment. There is no complete conducting path.
Correct. The gap breaks the complete path; its position after the resistor does not preserve current before it.
That was the current with a complete path. The break interrupts the entire steady loop.

hints: Identify whether any complete conducting path remains.
nodes.workedExample: If a single-loop wire breaks on either side of a load, the steady current is zero throughout that loop.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

nodes.title: Explain the repair
nodes.prompt: A 9 V supply and a 3 ohm resistor form a closed single loop. A technician says current is smaller after the resistor because some charge is used up. Choose the causal correction.

options.text: The supply creates extra charge to replace what the resistor consumes.
options.feedback: The source transfers energy; it does not continuously create net charge to replace consumed charge.

options.text: The current decreases the farther it travels from the supply.
options.feedback: Distance from the source does not cause steady current to vanish in this ideal single loop.

options.text: Charge is conserved. The resistor transfers energy; the steady current is the same before and after it.
options.feedback: Yes. Energy is transferred to the resistor. Charge flow does not steadily disappear along a single path.

hints: Distinguish charge from the energy transferred by each unit of charge.
nodes.workedExample: One path means no branch where charge can go elsewhere. In steady state, as much charge per second leaves the resistor as enters it.
nodes.mechanism: The supply transfers energy to charge already in the conducting circuit. A complete conducting path allows a steady current. The heater transfers energy, rather than consuming charge. In this one-path ideal circuit, the same current passes every point.
nodes.bridge: A steady current needs a complete conducting path. The source transfers energy; charge is conserved. You can return to the map and explore later.

debrief.title: The beacon has a story to tell
debrief.body: You investigated why the full path matters, and what the heater transfers.

nodes.title: The recorder needs a reading
nodes.prompt: A marker counts charge passing one point in a steady loop. Make 4 C pass it. Change the observation time or the resistor. Can you find two different settings that work?
hints: Current tells you how many coulombs pass each second. Compare 1 A for 4 s with 2 A for 2 s.
At 6 V, a 6 ohm resistor gives 1 A. A 3 ohm resistor gives 2 A in this ideal model.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V and 6 ohms, I = V/R = 1 A. In 4 s, Q = It = 4 C. At 3 ohms the current is 2 A, so 2 s also gives 4 C.
nodes.mechanism: Current is a rate of charge flow. The reading counts charge that passes a point during an interval, Q = It for a steady current. Charge is not used up by the resistor.
nodes.bridge: A closed path permits charge flow. Current says how fast charge passes a point; an observation window says for how long.

nodes.title: Longer watch, same flow
nodes.prompt: A different sensor carries a steady 1 A. The recorder watches one point for 6 s. What charge passes that point?

options.feedback: One ampere means 1 C each second. Six seconds counts six such intervals.
Yes. Q = It = 1 C/s times 6 s = 6 C.
Dividing by time would answer a different question. The total passing charge grows with the observation time.

hints: Write 1 A as 1 C per second, then count six seconds.
nodes.workedExample: If 2 A flows for 3 s, the charge passing the marker is 2 C/s times 3 s = 6 C.
nodes.mechanism: For steady flow, charge passing a point is current multiplied by elapsed time. A longer observation does not create charge; it counts more of the charge already flowing through the loop.
nodes.bridge: You can return to the circuit recorder or continue to a fresh measurement.

nodes.title: A new recorder trace
nodes.prompt: In another subsystem, 0.4 A passes a marker steadily for 15 s. How much charge passes it?

options.feedback: That divides current by time. Charge is the rate multiplied by the time.
Correct. 0.4 C/s times 15 s is 6 C.
That divides the 15 s by 0.4 A. The unit C/s times s gives C.

hints: An ampere is a coulomb per second. Multiply by the observation time.
nodes.workedExample: For 0.5 A over 8 s, Q = It = 0.5 C/s times 8 s = 4 C.
nodes.mechanism: The same rate-times-time relationship applies to an unfamiliar subsystem. A correct first attempt without revealed help is one piece of evidence, not a whole-skill certificate.
nodes.bridge: The total charge counted depends on both rate and duration. Next, reason about where that charge goes.

nodes.title: Where did the charge go?
nodes.prompt: A closed single-loop heater carries a steady 0.8 A into the resistor. What rate of charge leaves it at the other end?

options.text: Less than 0.8 A, because some charge becomes heat
options.feedback: The resistor transfers electrical energy to thermal energy. It does not consume charge in steady state.

options.text: 0.8 A, because charge is conserved in the single steady path
options.feedback: Yes. Equal charge per second enters and leaves the resistor in this steady single loop.

options.text: More than 0.8 A, because the source replaces charge
options.feedback: The source transfers energy to charge; it does not make extra steady current after the resistor.

hints: Separate the movement of charge from energy transferred to the heater.
nodes.workedExample: If 2 C enters a resistor in 2 s in a steady single loop, 2 C also leaves it in those 2 s. The current is 1 A on each side.
nodes.mechanism: A steady single path cannot accumulate charge indefinitely at the resistor. Current is equal around that path, while energy is transferred in the resistor.
nodes.bridge: The recorder gave you a rate and a total. The next investigation asks what energy each coulomb receives.

debrief.title: A useful rate
debrief.body: You used a charge counter to connect amperes, coulombs and seconds, then checked that the resistor transfers energy rather than consuming charge.

nodes.title: Set the energy lift
nodes.prompt: The console watches a 6 ohm ideal load for 4 s. Set the supply so each coulomb receives 6 J and the source transfers 24 J in the window. Explore what changes when the voltage changes.
hints: A potential difference of 1 V means 1 J transferred per coulomb. First find the setting that gives 6 J/C.
At 6 V across 6 ohms, the current is 1 A. In 4 s, 4 C passes the load.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V across 6 ohms, I = 1 A. In 4 s, Q = 4 C. Energy transferred is VQ = 6 J/C times 4 C = 24 J.
nodes.mechanism: Potential difference describes energy transferred per coulomb. Here the fixed ideal resistance also makes current change when voltage changes. Total energy over an interval depends on both the energy per charge and how much charge passes.
nodes.bridge: The recorder counted coulombs. Voltage now tells you the energy transferred for each coulomb.

nodes.title: Read a different lift
nodes.prompt: A source transfers 12 J to 2 C of charge. What potential difference did that charge cross?

options.feedback: Yes. 12 J divided by 2 C is 6 J/C, or 6 V.
That multiplies energy by charge. Potential difference is energy per unit charge.
That reverses the ratio. Divide energy by charge, not charge by energy.

hints: What does per coulomb mean in a numerical ratio?
nodes.workedExample: If 9 J is transferred to 3 C, the potential difference is 9 J / 3 C = 3 V.
nodes.mechanism: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, V = E/Q. It does not by itself tell you how much charge flows each second.
nodes.bridge: Now use the same principle with a new source rather than the console settings.

nodes.title: The backup source
nodes.prompt: The backup source transfers 15 J while 3 C passes through it. What is its potential difference?

options.feedback: That multiplies joules and coulombs. Volts are joules per coulomb.
Correct. 15 J / 3 C = 5 J/C = 5 V.
That divides 3 C by 15 J. The source's energy per coulomb is 15 divided by 3.

hints: Divide the transferred energy by the passing charge.
nodes.workedExample: If 20 J goes to 4 C, V = 20 J / 4 C = 5 V.
nodes.mechanism: The 5 V describes 5 J transferred for each coulomb. A different current could flow depending on the connected circuit.
nodes.bridge: Energy per charge and charge per second have different units and answer different questions.

nodes.title: Same rate, different lift?
nodes.prompt: Circuit A uses 6 V across 6 ohms. Circuit B uses 12 V across 12 ohms. Both are ideal single loops. Which statement is true?

options.text: Both have 1 A, so each coulomb receives the same energy
options.feedback: Both currents are 1 A, but the source potential differences are 6 J/C and 12 J/C.

options.text: The 12 V circuit must have twice the current
options.feedback: Its resistance also doubles. In each ideal loop, I = V/R = 1 A.

options.text: Both have 1 A, but each coulomb receives more energy in circuit B
options.feedback: Yes. The same charge per second passes, while circuit B supplies 12 J per coulomb rather than 6 J.

hints: Calculate V/R for each circuit, then compare the volts as joules per coulomb.
nodes.workedExample: A 4 V source across 4 ohms and an 8 V source across 8 ohms both give 1 A, but the energy supplied per coulomb is 4 J and 8 J respectively.
nodes.mechanism: Current and potential difference are distinct. The resistance determines how a particular ideal circuit responds to the source's energy per charge.
nodes.bridge: The next investigation lets you tune both supply and resistance to control current.

debrief.title: Energy for every coulomb
debrief.body: You linked volts to joules per coulomb and separated that idea from amperes, the rate of charge flow.

nodes.title: Keep the heater in range
nodes.prompt: The ideal sensor heater needs a steady 1 A. Tune supply voltage and resistance. There are two settings that work. Find both, then decide why they agree.
hints: For this ideal resistor, current is supply voltage divided by resistance.
A 6 V supply with 6 ohms gives the same current as 12 V with 12 ohms.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V and 6 ohms, I = V/R = 1 A. At 12 V and 12 ohms, I = 1 A again. The ratio stays equal even though voltage and resistance both change.
nodes.mechanism: In an ideal ohmic loop, I = V/R. At fixed voltage, more resistance means less current. If the supply voltage changes too, compare the whole ratio rather than one setting alone.
nodes.bridge: The source sets energy per charge; the load's ideal resistance determines the steady current for that voltage.

nodes.title: Two ways to one ampere
nodes.prompt: Why do both 6 V across 6 ohms and 12 V across 12 ohms produce 1 A in this ideal model?

options.text: An ideal source always supplies 1 A
options.feedback: The source fixes voltage here. Its current depends on the connected resistance.

options.text: Voltage and resistance rise together, leaving V/R at 1 A
options.feedback: Yes. 6/6 and 12/12 both equal 1 A.
Hold voltage at 6 V and change 6 ohms to 12 ohms: current falls from 1 A to 0.5 A.

hints: Calculate V/R for each setting rather than comparing voltage alone.
nodes.workedExample: At 8 V with 4 ohms, I = 2 A. At 16 V with 8 ohms, I = 2 A again.
nodes.mechanism: The same current can result from different pairs of voltage and resistance. This does not mean the source forces a constant current in every circuit.
nodes.bridge: Use a new supply setting to predict a change before viewing a readout.

nodes.title: A different heater
nodes.prompt: A 9 V ideal source drives a 3 ohm resistor. The resistor is replaced with 6 ohms while the source stays at 9 V. What is the new current?

options.feedback: Correct. 9 V / 6 ohms = 1.5 A, half the original 3 A.
That was the current with 3 ohms. At fixed voltage, doubling resistance halves current.
More resistance at the same voltage cannot double the current in this ideal ohmic circuit.

hints: Keep 9 V fixed and divide by the new 6 ohms.
nodes.workedExample: At 12 V, changing 4 ohms to 8 ohms changes current from 3 A to 1.5 A.
nodes.mechanism: The comparison holds voltage fixed. I = V/R gives 1.5 A after the resistance doubles.
nodes.bridge: The rule about resistance needs its fixed-voltage condition.

nodes.title: A rule with a condition
nodes.prompt: A colleague says: doubling resistance always halves current. Which correction fits ideal ohmic circuits?

options.text: The claim is true even if the supply voltage changes
options.feedback: If voltage doubles too, V/R and current can stay the same.

options.text: It is true when the potential difference is held fixed
options.feedback: Yes. I = V/R; at fixed V, doubling R halves I.
At a fixed source voltage, changing resistance changes current in this ideal model.

hints: Ask which quantity besides resistance appears in I = V/R.
nodes.workedExample: 6 V / 3 ohms = 2 A; 6 V / 6 ohms = 1 A. But 12 V / 6 ohms = 2 A again.
nodes.mechanism: Physics comparisons must state what stays fixed. The ideal resistor relation is useful within its model boundary, not a universal claim for every component.
nodes.bridge: Next, follow current and energy around a path with more than one load.

debrief.title: A ratio worth testing
debrief.body: You used voltage and resistance together to set current and qualified the fixed-voltage rule. The load is an ideal resistor, not a realistic lamp.

nodes.title: Tune two loads in one path
nodes.prompt: The station signal must run at 1 A through two ideal coils on one path. Set their resistances. Either coil can be the larger one. Compare the current and each voltage drop in the meter table before moving on.
hints: One path means both resistances contribute to the same total.
At 12 V, a total of 12 ohms gives 1 A. You can put 9 ohms in either coil.
nodes.workedExample: With 3 ohms and 9 ohms in series, total resistance is 12 ohms, so source current is 12 V / 12 ohms = 1 A. The same 1 A flows through both coils. Their voltage drops are 3 V and 9 V.
nodes.mechanism: In a steady one-path ideal circuit, charge has no junction at which to split, so current is the same in each load. Each load transfers a share of the source energy per charge; those voltage drops add to 12 V.
nodes.bridge: One path shares current. Voltage drops depend on each resistance and add back to the supply voltage.

nodes.title: Where does the energy go?
nodes.prompt: You found 1 A through a 3 ohm coil followed by a 9 ohm coil on a 12 V supply. Which pair of voltage drops should the meters show?

options.text: 3 V then 9 V; together they account for 12 V
options.feedback: Yes. With 1 A through each load, V = IR gives 3 V and 9 V. Their sum matches the source.

options.text: 6 V then 6 V because the source divides equally between two loads
options.feedback: Equal drops need equal resistances at the same current. These loads are 3 and 9 ohms.

options.text: 12 V across each coil because each receives the full supply
options.feedback: That describes parallel branches. These coils share one path, so their drops sum to 12 V.

hints: Use V = IR for each coil, then add the drops.
nodes.workedExample: At 1 A, a 2 ohm coil drops 2 V and a 10 ohm coil drops 10 V. The total is the 12 V supply.
nodes.mechanism: The source gives 12 J to each coulomb. The two loads together transfer that 12 J per coulomb, split in proportion to their resistances at the common current.
nodes.bridge: Series loads share current, but each load may transfer a different amount of energy per coulomb.

nodes.title: Turn the path around
nodes.prompt: The station asks whether position changes the current. Move the 9 ohm setting to the front and the 3 ohm setting to the rear. Compare the two meter rows; the first coil should now drop 9 V while source current stays 1 A.
hints: Change both coils so the total stays at 12 ohms.
With the front coil at 9 ohms and 1 A, it drops 9 V. The rear must be 3 ohms to keep 1 A.
nodes.workedExample: At 9 ohms plus 3 ohms, the total is still 12 ohms and the source still drives 1 A. The front now drops 9 V and the rear 3 V.
nodes.mechanism: Reordering ideal series loads changes where the voltage drops occur, not the total resistance or shared current. Real wires and non-ohmic devices can complicate this simple model.
nodes.bridge: Check a new path without relying on the old numbers.

nodes.title: A different station rail
nodes.prompt: A 15 V supply drives a 5 ohm load and a 10 ohm load in series. What current passes through the second load, and what potential difference is across it?

options.feedback: Correct. The total is 15 ohms, so both loads carry 1 A; the 10 ohm load drops 10 V.
The common current is 1 A, but 5 V is the drop across the 5 ohm load, not the 10 ohm load.
The 10 ohm load does not receive the full 15 V by itself. First add the series resistances: 5 + 10 = 15 ohms.

hints: Add the series resistances before dividing supply voltage by the total.
nodes.workedExample: For 18 V across 6 ohms and 3 ohms in series, total resistance is 9 ohms, current is 2 A and the 3 ohm load drops 6 V.
nodes.mechanism: One-path current is common to both loads. The drops are 5 V and 10 V, which account for the 15 V source.
nodes.bridge: Test whether the one-path rule survives a break.

nodes.title: One gap, two quiet loads
nodes.prompt: A connector between two ideal series loads opens. What happens to the steady current through the load before the gap and the load after it?

options.feedback: Yes. An open connection breaks the only complete path, so steady current stops everywhere in that path.

options.text: The first load still carries current, but the second does not
options.feedback: Charge cannot keep accumulating at the gap in this steady model. The whole single path is interrupted.

options.text: The second load still carries current from stored charge
options.feedback: Neither ideal resistor supplies charge or a closed return path. This model has no storage element.

hints: Trace a complete route from the source and back.
nodes.workedExample: If a switch opens anywhere in a single series loop, no complete conducting path remains, so current through every load is zero.
nodes.mechanism: A break in the only route stops the steady loop; contrast this with a later parallel circuit, where another complete branch may remain.
nodes.bridge: Next, let the station make two complete routes and see what a branch break changes.

debrief.title: One path, shared current
debrief.body: You changed resistance and watched one current pass through both ideal loads. Their potential differences divided the source energy per charge and added to the supply voltage.

nodes.title: Bring the backup branch online
nodes.prompt: The main rail runs through a 6 ohm ideal load at 6 V. The backup branch is open. Close its link and watch the source current and both branch currents. Then try reopening it; does the main branch go quiet?
hints: The open backup branch has no steady current, but the main branch still has a full route.
When both 6 ohm branches have 6 V across them, each carries 1 A; add them at the junction.
nodes.workedExample: Main alone: 6 V / 6 ohms = 1 A. Closing the backup makes a second 6 V / 6 ohm route carrying 1 A. The source supplies 2 A in total.
nodes.mechanism: Parallel branches share the same two junctions, so each ideal branch sees the full supply voltage. Charge flow into the split equals the sum of branch currents; an open backup does not break the intact main route.
nodes.bridge: Keep the backup open while you predict the main rail.

nodes.title: Does the main rail notice?
nodes.prompt: With two 6 ohm branches at 6 V, each carries 1 A. The backup link opens. What are the new main-branch and source currents in this ideal fixed-voltage circuit?

options.feedback: Exactly. The main branch still has 6 V across 6 ohms. Only the backup current disappears.
The backup has opened, but the main branch remains a complete route across the source.
The main branch still has 6 V across 6 ohms, so it remains at 1 A. Source current is now just that one branch.

hints: The ideal source holds 6 V across the still-complete main branch.
nodes.workedExample: At 10 V, a 5 ohm main branch stays at 2 A when a separate backup branch opens; source current loses only the backup contribution.
nodes.mechanism: For a fixed ideal source, removing one parallel route reduces source current, but need not change the voltage or current in another intact branch.
nodes.bridge: Now control which route consumes the current budget.

nodes.title: Spend only three amperes
nodes.prompt: Both station branches are complete at 12 V. At 6 ohms each, source current is 4 A. Adjust either branch so the total becomes 3 A, and compare the two ways to distribute it.
hints: At fixed 12 V, a 6 ohm branch takes 2 A and a 12 ohm branch takes 1 A.
Keep one branch at 6 ohms and set the other to 12 ohms. Swapping which branch is limited also works.
nodes.workedExample: At 12 V, the 6 ohm branch carries 2 A and the 12 ohm branch carries 1 A. The junction adds them to 3 A. Either branch can be the 12 ohm one.
nodes.mechanism: Changing one parallel branch changes that branch current and the source total. The other branch still sees the fixed 12 V in this ideal source model.
nodes.bridge: Make a fresh branch calculation without the visible readout.

nodes.title: A new junction
nodes.prompt: A 9 V ideal source feeds 3 ohms in one branch and 6 ohms in another. Both branches are complete. What current leaves the source?

options.feedback: Correct. The branch currents are 9/3 = 3 A and 9/6 = 1.5 A; together they are 4.5 A.
That is only the current through the 3 ohm branch. The source also feeds the 6 ohm branch.
That is only the current through the 6 ohm branch. Add the 3 A in the other branch.

hints: Each branch has 9 V across it. Find both currents, then add them.
nodes.workedExample: For two complete branches at 12 V with 4 ohms and 6 ohms, currents are 3 A and 2 A, so source current is 5 A.
nodes.mechanism: The 9 V source maintains the same potential difference across both ideal branches. Their separate charge-flow rates add at the source junction.
nodes.bridge: One last fault, this time with a surviving path.

nodes.title: A backup fuse opens
nodes.prompt: A 10 V ideal source feeds two complete branches: 5 ohms in the main branch and 10 ohms in the backup. The backup fuse opens. What happens to the main current and source total?

options.text: Main stays 2 A; source falls from 3 A to 2 A
options.feedback: Yes. Main remains at 10/5 = 2 A. The 1 A backup contribution disappears from the source total.

options.text: Main falls to 0 A; source falls to 0 A
options.feedback: The main branch is still a complete route across 10 V. Opening another branch does not break it.

options.text: Main rises to 3 A; source stays at 3 A
options.feedback: The ideal source holds the main branch at 10 V, so its 5 ohms still carry 2 A. The backup current no longer contributes.

hints: Check which route actually contains the open fuse.
nodes.workedExample: At 6 V, a 3 ohm main route carries 2 A even after a separate 6 ohm backup route opens; the source total falls from 3 A to 2 A.
nodes.mechanism: Conservation holds at the split: source current is the sum of complete-branch currents. A break removes its branch contribution without consuming charge in the other route.
nodes.bridge: The next investigation will ask which meter reading can distinguish a fault from a normal load change.

debrief.title: More than one way home
debrief.body: You kept an intact branch running while another opened, and balanced source current as the sum of separate branch currents. The ideal source held each branch at the same voltage.

scopeNote: Partial pilot: 6 of 10 planned investigations. The ideal DC resistor/switch model supports bounded series and parallel trees, not transients, realistic lamps or unrestricted electronics. Measurement, power budgeting, faults, an open workspace and capstone remain planned.
